name: FTP
summary: The File Transfer Protocol: text commands on a control connection to port 21, and a second TCP connection for every listing or file. Everything, passwords included, travels unencrypted.
intro: An FTP client opens a TCP connection to the server’s port 21 and holds a conversation in Telnet-style text lines: `USER` and `PASS` to log in, `CWD` to change directory, `TYPE A` or `TYPE I` for text or binary, `LIST` for a directory listing, `RETR` to download and `STOR` to upload, each answered with a three-digit reply code. The files themselves never cross that control connection. For every transfer a separate data connection is opened. In active mode the client announces an address and port with `PORT` and the server connects back to it, by default from its port 20. In passive mode the client sends `PASV`, the server replies with an address and port it is listening on, and the client connects out to it. Passive mode gets through firewalls more easily because the client makes both connections outward, so clients such as curl use it by default. `EPRT` and `EPSV` (RFC 2428) extend both to IPv6.

In ASCII mode the sender converts text to a standard form with CRLF line endings and the receiver converts it to its own, which damages a binary file sent that way; image mode (`TYPE I`) sends bytes untouched. Standard FTP sends all data and control information, including passwords, unencrypted, and an FTP server can be told with `PORT` to connect to a third machine, the basis of the “bounce attack”. FTPS (FTP over TLS) adds encryption to the same protocol; SFTP, despite its name, is a different protocol that runs over SSH. Chrome 88 removed FTP support from the browser entirely.
strengths: Easy to script: command-line tools such as curl speak FTP and FTPS, and a transfer is a few text commands
One login covers a whole session: list, upload and download many files, restart an interrupted transfer (`REST`) or abort one (`ABOR`)
Anonymous FTP made public archives easy: anyone can log in as `anonymous` and download
limits: No encryption: user names, passwords and file contents cross the network in plain text
The second connection on a negotiated port is awkward for firewalls and NAT; active mode often fails outright from behind them
ASCII mode changes line endings, so a binary file sent as text arrives corrupted
Weak by design against abuse: `PORT` enables bounce attacks, and the base standard allows unlimited password guesses
Browsers no longer support it: Chrome removed FTP in version 88

story: FTP is older than TCP. In April 1971 Abhay Bhushan at MIT Project MAC proposed a File Transfer Protocol (RFC 114) so that users could work with the file systems of other ARPANET hosts without logging in to them, starting with MIT’s Multics and ITS machines. A long series of RFCs revised it through the 1970s, and when the ARPANET moved from NCP to TCP, FTP was rebuilt for TCP as RFC 765. Jon Postel and Joyce Reynolds’s RFC 959 (October 1985) corrected and extended that edition, adding commands such as `MKD`, `PWD` and `CDUP`, and has been the base specification ever since.

Anonymous FTP archive sites, open to anyone who logged in as `anonymous`, offered a wealth of public software and documents; RFC 1635 (1994) explained how to use them. The protocol’s design then aged badly. Firewalls blocked the server’s connection back to the client, so RFC 1579 (1994) recommended that clients use `PASV`. RFC 2577 (1999) documented the bounce attack and password guessing, and noted that standard FTP sends everything unencrypted. Security was added on top as FTPS rather than changed in FTP itself, and browsers eventually dropped the protocol.

choices.why: Commands and replies stay on one connection while each file flows on its own, so a client can keep talking to the server, list directories and start or abort transfers independently of the data.

choices.choice: The server connects back by default
choices.why: In RFC 959 the server initiates the data connection to a port the user side listens on. That worked while hosts could reach each other directly, and became FTP’s main problem once packet-filtering firewalls blocked incoming calls to unknown ports, which is why RFC 1579 told clients to use passive mode.

Hosts on the network stored text differently (RFC 959 still defines both ASCII and EBCDIC types), so FTP defined a standard text form that each side converts to and from, plus an image type for raw bytes.
